OK Military academy merger still raises doubts : The latest proposal for a unified armed forces academy raises concerns over shifting plans, political motives and military readiness The Democratic Party (DP) and the Defense Ministry unveiled a revised plan on Wednesday to establish a unified military academy by merging the Army, Navy and Air Force academies. Under the proposal, first-year and fourth-year cadets would receive joint training at a new academy in Daejeon's Jaun military complex, while each service would oversee second-year and third-year education. The Army Academy would relocate from the Taereung area of Nowon District, northern Seoul, to the central Chungcheong region, while the Navy and Air Force academies would retain their existing facilities in Jinhae and Cheongju, respectively. The revision follows criticism of the original plan to provide four years of joint education at a location with access to neither the sea nor an airstrip. If the relevant legislation is amended, the three existing academies would disappear, replaced by separate service divisions within the unified institution. Military authorities argue that integration is necessary to prepare officers for future battlefields. They also cite urban development around the current campus, which has restricted training facilities, as justification for relocation. Yet fundamental questions remain. The military has offered insufficient explanation of how future warfare will change. Without an accurate diagnosis, how can policymakers devise an effective solution? Moreover, the government's proposal has changed twice in seven months. An April plan for two years of joint education became a four-year program in July before the latest revision was revealed. Such repeated changes suggest improvised policymaking rather than thorough preparation for restructuring an 80-year-old military education system. The Ministry of National Defense now promises research by specialized institutions and discussions with experts on detailed curricula. But conducting such studies only after deciding to relocate the current academy reinforces suspicions that the government has predetermined its preferred outcome. Consequently, doubts persist that the merger is intended to erase the military academy's institutional identity because some of its graduates were implicated in the Dec. 3, 2024, martial law crisis. Among countries maintaining standing forces of at least 300,000 troops, only a handful, including Thailand and Venezuela, operate unified military academies. North Korea, meanwhile, maintains specialized institutions for training Army officers in fields such as special operations and artillery. Reforming the system that develops Korea's future military leadership must be guided by national security requirements, not partisan political objectives. Such far-reaching changes demand rigorous analysis, meaningful consultation and public confidence. The government must demonstrate how integration will strengthen military capabilities rather than merely reorganize institutions. Without convincing evidence and broad consensus, the latest proposal risks deepening distrust instead of delivering the military education reforms Korea needs. That responsibility cannot be left to improvisation. South Korean first lady Kim Hea Kyung has charmed Chinese social media users with her warmth towards ground staff, personal style and affection for her husband – fuelling online “shipping” of Seoul’s first couple.

Like other visiting dignitaries, Lee and Kim received a red-carpet welcome with an honour guard. More than 100 dancers dressed in white shirts and pink skirts waved flower bouquets and danced on the tarmac.

But what caught attention on Chinese social media was the South Korean first couple’s reactions to those greeting them.

Lee and Kim began to applaud the greeters as they walked on the red carpet, and Kim continued to clap her hands and wave at the staff behind her car’s tinted closed window once inside.

![Image 1: South Korean President Lee Jae Myung and first lady Kim Hea Kyung arrive at Shenzhen Baoan International Airport on Wednesday for the Apec leaders’ meeting. Photo: AFP](https://img.i-scmp.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=contain,width=1024,format=auto/sites/default/files/d8/images/canvas/2026/11/19/883c2358-700a-480f-aa0f-d5c350aa7c62_c5892012.jpg)

South Korean President Lee Jae Myung and first lady Kim Hea Kyung arrive at Shenzhen Baoan International Airport on Wednesday for the Apec leaders’ meeting. Photo: AFP

In a social media post, one commenter said the couple’s conduct showed “none of the anticipated solemnity or stiffness”, singling out the applause that went on for several seconds and their eyes “brimming with genuine gratitude”.

The post described the South Korean first lady as showing “natural poise and ease that simply cannot be faked”.

“Accustomed as we are to the meticulously choreographed protocols of diplomatic occasions and the grand narratives of major-power rivalry, we often overlook these small yet heartwarming moments,” the commenter added.

“The true essence of international relations can be the simplest goodwill between people.”

Beyond her warm gestures, Kim has also drawn praise for her attire: a light pink dress upon stepping off the aircraft, a light green traditional Korean hanbok for a lunch later in the day and a white hanbok at the welcome dinner.

Seoul’s first lady has a large fan base in China, with a dedicated “super topic” on [Weibo](https://www.scmp.com/topics/weibo?module=inline&pgtype=article), one of China’s largest social media platforms. The feature allows users of the site to build and join interest-based communities. Another super topic dedicated to the presidential couple has drawn thousands of followers and posts.

In these online communities, users praise Kim’s style, closely track her schedule and share photos of the couple’s public interactions.

Some have taken to affectionately calling Lee and Kim “Mom and Dad”, a term used by “shippers” – fans who cheer a couple’s romance – to express their fondness for the two.

Fans in these channels have also written fan fiction about the couple, with some even using photos of the pair as their phone-lock screens.

On Wednesday, Lee and Chinese President [Xi Jinping](https://www.scmp.com/topics/xi-jinping?module=inline&pgtype=article) held talks, with Xi urging his counterpart to safeguard global supply chains, deepen economic policy coordination and foster cooperation on [artificial intelligence](https://www.scmp.com/topics/artificial-intelligence?module=inline&pgtype=article).

Xbox Q1 FY2027 Earnings Breakdown: What a $5.38 Billion Quarter and Slowing Hardware Losses Say About Microsoft’s Gaming Reset
theblowup/unsplash.com Xbox generated $5.38 billion in gaming revenue during the July–September 2026 quarter, a 2% drop year-over-year , yet buried beneath the headline decline is a development worth watching closely: the console revenue freefall is decelerating in a meaningful way, and Microsoft's own quarterly reporting shows first-party content turning positive for the first time during this downturn cycle .
After years of mounting losses across hardware and software, Q1 FY2027 may mark the period where Microsoft's Xbox reset stops getting worse — though whether the coming months can convert that into actual growth remains the central open question for the division.
A Controlled Decline, Not Yet a Recovery
The figures released Wednesday as part of Microsoft's quarterly earnings describe deceleration, not reversal — but for an Xbox division that logged hardware revenue collapses of 29%, 32%, and 33% across the first three quarters of fiscal 2026, a 14% hardware decline in Q1 FY2027 reads as fragile, hard-earned progress.
The $129 million total shortfall came from two sources: a hardware segment still bleeding volume as the Xbox Series X|S cycle ages toward a generational replacement, and a content-and-services line that slipped 2% overall — reversing the slim 1% gain it posted during the same period a year ago. However, Microsoft's Form 10-Q filing shows that first-party content revenue actually grew during the quarter, with the drag coming entirely from Game Pass and third-party titles. That distinction carries weight for the recovery thesis: it means Microsoft's own studios are beginning to show up on the ledger in a positive way even as the subscription and licensing lines remain under pressure.
What Microsoft's Broader Numbers Look Like
The gaming shortfall arrives against a sharply different backdrop at the company level. Total Microsoft revenue reached $92.3 billion for the quarter, a 19% year-over-year increase , while net income climbed 32% to $36.6 billion. Azure cloud services grew 48% year-over-year — the fastest growth rate Azure has recorded in years — and Microsoft 365 commercial cloud revenue rose 17% on a reported basis.
Xbox's struggles, in other words, remain a contained wound on an otherwise thriving corporate body. But for a company that spent tens of billions assembling the Activision Blizzard portfolio and built the world's largest gaming subscription service, persistent gaming drag carries strategic weight that exceeds its proportional revenue share.
The 14% hardware decline in Q1 FY2027 is the most modest quarterly contraction for Xbox console revenue since the current downturn took hold. For context, fiscal year 2026 saw hardware revenue fall $1.7 billion overall , with consecutive quarterly contractions of 29%, 32%, and 33% through the first three quarters of the year, before a partial easing to 13% in the final quarter.
The moderating trajectory is partly a base-effect math problem correcting itself: the prior-year comparisons no longer run against stronger console volume periods. Meanwhile, Project Helix — Microsoft's publicly confirmed codename for its next-generation console — is in development with alpha hardware slated to reach developers in 2027, while a consumer launch is widely expected no earlier than the holiday 2027 window. There is no structural hardware relief arriving before then, making execution on software the primary lever available to the division in the near term.
Content and Services: First-Party Light in a Mixed Picture
The content and services line is where the clearest division between positive and negative signals sits. The segment's 2% overall decline in Q1 FY2027 masks an internal split: first-party content contributed positively to the quarter while Game Pass subscriptions and third-party licensing fell short . That trajectory matters because content and services had been the one pillar holding positive while hardware crumbled — it turned negative in Q2 FY2026, worsened to -10% by Q4 FY2026, and the current quarter's -2% suggests some stabilization even if the overall direction remains red.
The Q2 Release Slate Has Already Started Landing
Three of the titles central to Microsoft's near-term revenue recovery are no longer upcoming — they have already launched. Halo: Campaign Evolved, the full remake of the original 2001 game, launched July 28, 2026 — within the Q1 FY2027 reporting window — making its day-one Game Pass impact a factor already captured in the numbers released Wednesday. Gears of War: E-Day followed with a full release on October 6, 2026 , landing as an Xbox console exclusive with Game Pass day-one access and strong early reception. And Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 shipped October 23, 2026 across PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X|S, PC, and Nintendo Switch 2 — though notably, Microsoft elected not to include it on Xbox Game Pass at launch, a departure from its recent Activision Blizzard strategy that limits its immediate subscription uplift.
The release that has yet to hit shelves is the one Microsoft appears most focused on commercially. The legislation has drawn outcry from legal and anti-corruption experts, climate groups, crossbenchers and civil liberties organisations, after the high court ruled last month that an approval for an expansion that would increase the mine’s annual output to 21MT until 2048 was invalid.
In a 3-2 split ruling, the high court found the state’s Independent Planning Commission (IPC) failed to properly consider imposing conditions to minimise greenhouse gas emissions that would be generated by the mine when the coal is sold and burned overseas.

An on-duty police officer has been shot and a man found dead nearby as police investigate two firearm incidents in a tiny Tasmanian town.
The officer was working at Whitemark police station on Flinders Island, north-east of the island of Tasmania, when he was shot at about 9.45pm on Saturday night.
Police sent to investigate the shooting of the officer discovered the body of a man, believed to be in his mid-20s, with a gunshot wound on Walker Street, near the police station.
“At this time, police believe these two incidents are linked and that the situation has been safely contained,” Tasmanian police said in a statement on Sunday.
“Our thoughts are with the families and loved ones of those involved, and with the wider community of Flinders Island.”
The policeman is receiving treatment at the Royal Hobart hospital and remains in a serious but stable condition.
Whitemark has a population of about 300 according to the 2021 census, and the entire population of Flinders Island is fewer than 1,000 people.
Extra police resources, including forensic and uniformed officers, have been deployed to the island. Those with information about these incidents, including CCTV or dashcam footage of Walker Street, have been urged to contact police.
It is the second shooting of an on-duty police officer in Tasmania in 18 months. A Tasmanian officer was killed in the state’s north-west in June 2025 while executing a court-issued warrant to repossess a residence. The occupant of the home pleaded guilty to murder.

IT·SCIENCE Call of Duty removes Itaewon crowd crush footage after backlash by Lee Junyoung Published : Oct. 30, 2026 - 16:00:14 View Korean Original
Opening cinematic used real news footage from the 2022 Itaewon crowd crush
Developer Activision issues formal apology, announces deletion of footage
Government had raised possibility of sanctions before resolution
Activision has announced it will remove footage from the opening sequence of Call of Duty that sparked controversy over its apparent use of real news footage from the Itaewon crowd crush.
The game, which centers on a fictional North Korean invasion of South Korea, drew immediate criticism after its launch over allegations that its opening cinematic incorporated actual broadcast footage from the October 2022 Itaewon crowd crush.
After the South Korean government raised the possibility of sanctions, Activision ultimately issued a formal apology and announced it would delete the disputed footage.
Activision said in an official statement Friday that "the footage in question will be completely removed through a game update to be distributed on Nov. 12." The company also offered a formal apology to the bereaved families and victims of the Itaewon crowd crush, saying it "bows its head in deep condolence and apology."
Earlier, the company had said it had "no intention of evoking any tragic event, including the Itaewon crowd crush, or of minimizing the pain it caused," while stopping short of committing to removing the disputed footage. As criticism mounted, Activision decided to delete the footage just one week after the game's launch.
Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 is a first-person war shooter Activision released Saturday. The Call of Duty franchise is a globally popular series that has surpassed $40 billion in cumulative sales worldwide, with more than 500 million copies sold as of 2024. According to gaming statistics site SteamDB, the latest installment shot straight to the top of the weekly most-played games chart.
The game drew controversy in South Korea from the moment of its release. The initial flashpoint was its use of a Korean War setting and a storyline depicting a North Korean invasion of the South, with critics arguing it was inappropriate to use an ongoing conflict as entertainment material.
The backlash intensified when it emerged that the game's opening cinematic appeared to include actual broadcast footage from the Itaewon crowd crush. The disputed scenes showed paramedics carrying stretchers and performing CPR — imagery strongly reminiscent of the disaster.
The controversy prompted the government to raise the possibility of sanctions. Ministry of Interior and Safety Minister Yun Ho-jung, speaking at a press briefing at Government Complex Sejong on Thursday, characterized the use of the footage as "secondary harm" to victims and said "there should be appropriate sanctions for this."
Yun added that "it seems like a matter for the relevant authorities to decide — whether to impose penalties or to block access to the game."
Activision's announcement came just one day after those remarks, and the government appears to consider the matter resolved for now. The Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism oversees domestic game industry policy and game content regulations. The ministry said Friday that following Activision's deletion and apology, "the relevant department regards this as a concluded matter."
The Game Rating and Administration Committee, which operates under the Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism, said it "sympathizes with the gravity of the issue and the concerns raised, and has been closely monitoring the situation," but added that it "has not discussed any specific sanctions, such as blocking access to the game."

sources.text:

Published Time: 2026-11-22T20:00:07+08:00

Markdown Content:
Small multirotor and first-person view [drones](https://www.scmp.com/topics/drones?module=inline&pgtype=article) are now widely used – and one of the most challenging new threats – on the modern battlefield.

These drones are small, they fly at low altitudes usually off the traditional air defence radars, and combined with their manoeuvrability they are difficult to detect. A camera on an FPV drone gives the operator a live video feed that can be viewed through goggles, a headset or screen.

These drones can be used for precision strikes against personnel, vehicles and other battlefield assets. But given their relatively low cost they are often used in large numbers to carry out swarm attacks and can also be deployed to overwhelm air defences in a saturation attack.

While they may be relatively vulnerable to soft-kill and hard-kill attacks, countering them – especially in a swarm – requires rapid detection and response, flexible deployment, and a low cost per engagement. And ideally, countermeasures should be able to engage multiple targets simultaneously and sustain operations against repeated waves of attacks.

One way to do that is to combine soft-kill electronic warfare (EW), directed-energy weapons such as lasers and microwaves, and kinetic interceptors.

China has developed a range of EW systems to disrupt command-and-control links and satellite-navigation signals used by small unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs).

They include the vehicle-mounted JN-1101, developed by China Electronics Technology Group Corporation, and the integrated counter-unmanned aircraft system suite CEW-102E introduced by Poly Defence in 2024.

At the tactical level, Chinese defence contractors have developed a range of portable anti-drone jammers – such as the DZ-02 Pro by Shen Zhou Ming Da High Technology – allowing individual operators to rapidly respond to incursions.

These soft-kill systems usually combine radar, electro-optical sensors, radio frequency detection and jamming capabilities.

![Image 1: The OW5-A50, developed by Norinco, is a high-energy laser air defence system. Photo: Sohu](https://img.i-scmp.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=contain,width=1024,format=auto/sites/default/files/d8/images/canvas/2026/11/21/f9e9993d-0413-4a40-bfc9-9af63bb612b4_168979fe.jpg)

The OW5-A50, developed by Norinco, is a high-energy laser air defence system. Photo: Sohu

High-energy laser weapons deliver low-cost engagements, rapid firing cycles, and virtually unlimited ammunition – only subject to power availability. Several Chinese-made high-energy laser systems have reportedly entered service with the [People’s Liberation Army](https://www.scmp.com/topics/china-military?module=inline&pgtype=article) and gained traction in the international arms market.

The OW5 series, developed by Norinco, was among the systems showcased at China’s high-profile Victory Day military parade in September 2025. The Guangjian, or Light Arrow family, developed by the Aviation Industry Corporation of China, has also featured prominently in PLA counter-drone exercises.

Meanwhile, the LW series by China Aerospace Science and Industry Corporation – including the LW-30, which is marketed internationally as Silent Hunter – and the SkyShield and SkyDome series by CETC have reportedly been exported to several countries such as Saudi Arabia and Oman. Some of these systems have also reportedly shot down drones in combat.

The PLA Navy has unveiled a shipborne high-energy laser weapon, designated LY-1, with higher power output than these truck-mounted systems. It is designed to defend against incoming drones and missiles at close range.

Photograph: Andriy Popov/Alamy Pip review will call for overhaul rather than scrapping benefit for under-25s Recommendations overseen by Stephen Timms would retain system for all ages, unlike last week’s Milburn review A long-awaited review of the personal independence payment (Pip) system will this week recommend that it is overhauled, a week after another report called for it to be partly scrapped. The final report on Pip by a committee co-led by Stephen Timms, the social security minister, is expected to be published as soon as Tuesday, presenting Andy Burnham with one of his most politically sensitive decisions yet as prime minister. Its conclusions, shaped with the input of disability rights advocates, are understood to be very similar to a draft set of recommendations that emerged in September, which called for a series of changes, particularly to the system of assessment, to take better account of conditions that vary over time. This would involve significant changes to Pip, which is intended to help disabled people meet the extra costs of disability. An interim report by Timms’ committee described the benefit as widely valued but “no longer fit for purpose”. However, it would retain the system for all ages, while last week’s report by Alan Milburn on worklessness among young people called for it to be scrapped for adults under 25 and replaced by an “additional cost allowance”, part of a wider network of job-based help for this age group. Government officials have pushed back on the idea of a clash, saying Milburn’s review was commissioned after the Timms process had begun, and that about 90% of the Pip caseload involves people over 25. But with Timms’ recommendations understood to be quite broad, Burnham and his ministers will need to make a series of decisions about what comes next, on a deeply sensitive subject. Keir Starmer was forced to abandon planned changes in 2025 after a rebellion by Labour MPs. Age instead of need drives Alan Milburn’s new reforms. The spacecraft BepiColombo is seen at the European Space Agency's (ESA) European Space Research and Technology Centre (ESTEC) in Noordwijk, Netherlands July 6, 2017. REUTERS/Michael Kooren
Nov 22 : After an eight-year journey, the European-Japanese spacecraft BepiColombo has begun orbiting the solar system's smallest and innermost planet Mercury, though the European Space Agency said on Sunday a glitch has occurred involving its thrusters.
Mercury, only slightly larger than Earth's moon, is the least explored of the four planets in the inner solar system, with BepiColombo only the third spacecraft to visit the planet and just the second to orbit it.
It is a joint mission of the European Space Agency, or ESA, and the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency, or JAXA.
ESA confirmed on Saturday that BepiColombo had begun its orbit. In a social media post on Sunday, ESA said the spacecraft had a successful entry into orbit, but during the maneuver, "the thruster burn was shorter than planned following a software issue."

The robotic spacecraft, launched in 2018, is a composite of ESA's Mercury Planetary Orbiter and JAXA's Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter, which have different scientific objectives and are due to separate on December 9 and 10. Routine science operations are slated to commence in April.
The mission will seek to answer questions about Mercury such as why it has a magnetic field, why ice exists in the polar craters of a sun-scorched planet, and what is the nature of enigmatic depressions called "hollows" on its surface.
Mercury's surface looks similar to that of the moon, with numerous impact craters. There are expanses of smooth terrain as well as cliffs, some up to a mile (1.6 km) tall.
Mercury is about 60 per cent closer to the sun than Earth. That means that from its surface, the sun appears more than three times as large and seven times as luminous as it does when seen from Earth. Mercury's diameter of 3,032 miles (4,880 km) is less than 40 per cent of Earth's diameter of 7,926 miles (12,753 km).

United States Files Action to Recover More Than $1 Billion in Cryptocurrency Assets Stolen by North Korean Cyber Actors in Binance Hack
Today, the Justice Department announced actions taken to forfeit over $1.1 billion in cryptocurrency that was criminally obtained by North Korean actors from Binance last month. This is part of the greater government effort to assist Binance in recovering over $6 billion in stolen assets. To date, the United States has assisted in the freezing, seizing, and/or the return of over $2.9 billion worth of cryptocurrency from multiple sources since the theft from Binance on or about Oct. 29.
“This forfeiture action is the latest example of our efforts to combat the North Korean government’s attempts to profit from the injustices it repeatedly inflicts upon innocent victims,” said Acting Principal Deputy Assistant Attorney General for National Security M. Scott Proctor. “The Department of Justice has long prioritized victims and their rights, and the commencement of this forfeiture action so soon after the restraint of these same assets reflects our commitment to ensuring that victims remain at the forefront of our work.”
“North Korean cyber hackers stole more than $6 billion in cryptocurrency from Binance, but swift coordination between the government and private sector partners helped prevent a substantial portion of those assets from disappearing,” said Assistant Attorney General A. A person who posted defamatory comments about victims of the Itaewon crowd crush has been fined 3 million won ($2,240).
According to legal sources, Judge Kim Su-jeong of the Yeoju Branch of Suwon District Court sentenced the defendant, identified only as A, to the fine in late August on charges of defaming the deceased.
A was indicted on charges of posting comments under a news article about the disaster on Oct. 30, 2022 — the day after the Itaewon crowd crush — that falsely impugned the victims' character and motives for attending the event.
Investigators determined that A had publicly stated false facts, damaging the honor of those who died in the Itaewon crowd crush, and brought charges under the Criminal Act's provision on defamation of the deceased.
The court agreed that the charges were substantiated.
In reaching its verdict, the court reviewed as established facts the circumstances surrounding the Itaewon crowd crush, including investigation outcomes and court rulings related to the inadequate response by the Yongsan Police Station chief and others.
The court found that A "publicly stated false facts, thereby defaming the victims of the Itaewon crowd crush."
On sentencing, the court said it took into account that the offense was a one-time act, that A had no prior criminal record, and that A had shown remorse.
The ruling is now final. Neither the prosecution nor A filed an appeal against the first-instance verdict.
Meanwhile, the first custodial sentence in a defamation-of-the-deceased case involving Itaewon crowd crush victims was handed down in June. Facebook Twitter Print Email UN chief urges talks on global AI safety framework, warns of historic shift in power Special coverage 23 November 2026 Economic Development UN Secretary-General António Guterres on Monday called on Member States to begin discussions on a multilateral framework for managing the risks of artificial intelligence (AI), warning that the technology is driving “the biggest transfer of power in the history of humankind”. Speaking to reporters at the close of the Bridgetown Special Summit on AI Safety in Barbados, Mr. Guterres – who leaves office at the end of December – said protections against AI risks remain fragmented and too often, governments “are playing catch-up”. “That is why today we are issuing a call from Bridgetown for Member States to begin discussions on a multilateral AI Risk Management Framework ,” he said. “Put simply, we need a common foundation for AI safety .” This includes: shared safety measures
independent evaluation and oversight of advanced AI models
support so that every country can put them into practice
The summit co-hosted by the UN and Barbados, comes as some of the leading AI developers are themselves sounding the alarm about increasingly powerful systems , Mr. Guterres said.
Recent technological outages and cyberattacks have exposed the vulnerabilities of the digital systems the world increasingly depends on , he warned, and AI is amplifying the threats, with systems behaving in ways “even their developers did not always anticipate”.
“We have a responsibility to take those warnings seriously. Not to stop innovation or spread fear. But to ensure that our capacity to manage this technology keeps pace with the technology itself,” he said.
Opening the summit, he stated that the promise of AI is real , from strengthening health systems to accelerating scientific discovery, but the risks of unchecked digital technology “are growing just as fast”.
He described the dangers as: “Technology without accountability. Capability without safeguards. And power without responsibility.”
During a fireside conversation with Barbadian Prime Minister Mia Mottley, Mr. Guterres said that while power once shifted among countries, it is now moving “from States, from governing institutions to a small number of companies and persons” ; a shift for which institutions created after the Second World War, including the UN, are “today not adequately equipped”.

At the first Global Dialogue on AI Governance in July, 111 of the participating countries had never taken part in any discussion on AI, he noted.

Australians to gain right to sue social media giants under Labor-Greens deal
Anika Wells says the government has reached a deal with the Greens on a digital duty of care. ( ABC News: Matt Roberts )
Labor has secured support for laws requiring social media companies to do more to protect Australians online.
The deal gives people the right to take tech giants to court over harm they suffer.
The digital duty of care legislation is due to pass the Senate with the Greens' support.
Australians will be able to directly sue social media giants for harm under changes to the federal government's proposed new digital safety laws.
Labor reached a deal with the Greens today to pass its digital duty of care legislation through the Senate, after agreeing to a series of amendments to increase penalties and give people greater power to hold tech giants to account.
The government agreed to give Australians a "private right of action" that would allow them to sue social media companies for harm suffered online.
Australia's current online safety laws largely rely on the eSafety commissioner to hold tech companies to account, leaving individuals seeking compensation to navigate complex and largely untested avenues under existing negligence and consumer protection laws.
The Greens say social media companies need to "dump the doomscroll". ( ABC News: Michael Franchi )
In the United States, where courts have greater scope to award damages designed to punish companies as well as compensate victims, thousands of lawsuits have been brought against social media giants.
In one landmark case this year, a jury awarded $US6 million (almost $9 million) to a young woman who suffered harm from social media addiction.
Social media companies to face higher fines
Under Labor's deal with the Greens, the maximum penalty for breaching the duty would be raised to up to 5 per cent of a platform's global revenue, rather than Labor's initial proposal of up to $109.2 million.
The amendments also grant the government rule-making powers to establish a digital complaints ombudsman in the future to handle small claims and resolve minor issues.
Social media users will be able to switch off their algorithms under the new laws. ( ABC News: Abbey Haberecht )
Labor's proposed duty would require online platforms such as Facebook, TikTok and Instagram to take reasonable steps to prevent a range of harms to children, including bullying, misogyny and content promoting eating disorders.
Big tech would also have to limit adults' exposure to serious harms such as threats of violence, stalking and the non-consensual sharing of intimate images.
The bill would also let Australians aged 16 and over switch off algorithm-driven feeds and see only content from accounts they chose to follow.
Greens say duty changes take power 'back' from big tech
Greens leader David Shoebridge said the amendments his party secured were "taking power back" from largely US-based corporations on behalf of Australians.
"This is a powerful demonstration of how you get results in politics," he said.
"As Greens, we have campaigned for a duty of care for years and now we will help deliver laws with real teeth that put people ahead of big tech profits."
Sarah Hanson-Young has fought for bigger fines tied to tech giants' global revenue. ( ABC News: Matt Roberts )
Greens communications spokeswoman Sarah Hanson-Young said social media giants would pay billions of dollars for the harm they caused.
"Like every other company selling products in Australia, big tech will finally be held responsible for the harm that their products cause," Senator Hanson-Young said.
"Just like food producers and toy manufacturers, big tech will not get away with creating products that put people at risk."

Active-Duty U.S. Army Sergeant Pleads Guilty in Conspiracy to Gather and Transfer National Defense Information
Jian Zhao, 37, an active-duty U.S. Army sergeant stationed at Joint Base Lewis-McChord in Washington, pleaded guilty yesterday to conspiring to gather, transmit and transfer national defense information to individuals connected to China.
“Members of the U.S. military are entrusted with protecting some of our nation’s most sensitive information and capabilities,” said U.S. Attorney Scott E. Bradford for the District of Oregon. “The defendant violated that trust by exploiting his access to military information and equipment for personal profit while knowingly providing materials to individuals linked to China. Protecting our national security depends on holding accountable those who compromise their oath and endanger the security of our armed forces.”
“By his own admission, Jian Zhao - a member of the U.S. Armed Forces - betrayed the country he swore an oath to defend by providing the Chinese government with sensitive U.S. military information,” said Assistant Director Roman Rozhavsky of the FBI’s Counterintelligence and Espionage Division. “Protecting our military’s technological advantage over our adversaries is one of the FBI’s highest priorities, and we rely on our partners on the National Counterintelligence Task Force to help us keep our warfighters and the American people safe. Let this guilty plea be a warning to any U.S. service members considering betraying our country: The FBI and our partners will find you and hold you accountable.”
According to court documents, Zhao enlisted in the U.S. Army in 2017 and served as a Battery Supply Sergeant. As part of his duties, Zhao maintained a security clearance and had authorized access to sensitive military information and equipment.
Beginning around November 2021 and continuing through March 2025, Zhao conspired with Ruoyu Duan, a former U.S. Army soldier living in Hillsboro, Oregon, and others to obtain and transfer information and equipment related to the national defense to buyers in China. Duan, who previously pleaded guilty to conspiracy to transmit national defense information, recruited active-duty U.S. military personnel, including Zhao, to provide defense-related information and facilitated communications and financial transactions with China-based purchasers.
As part of the conspiracy, Zhao provided excerpts from technical manuals related to the High Mobility Artillery Rocket System, offered military computers and government hard drives for sale and photographed restricted military presentations and documents concerning U.S. Army operations, communications networks, rocket and missile systems and military exercises.
Zhao also sold military materials he described as sensitive, secret or top secret and received thousands of dollars in payments from overseas buyers. He also removed government property and military storage devices without authorization and photographed controlled military documents using his personal cell phone.
On March 6, 2025, federal agents arrested Zhao at his residence in Lacey, Washington, where they recovered approximately $30,000 in cash, electronic devices and multiple Army hard drives.
Under the terms of the plea agreement, Zhao agreed to forfeit $17,500 as proceeds of the offense and abandon his interest in approximately $30,000 seized during the investigation.

China has launched an investigation into Shanghai’s Communist party chief Chen Jining, a member of the country’s elite politburo, the state-run Xinhua news agency unexpectedly announced on Tuesday, marking the fourth member of the top leadership ⁠body to be probed since ⁠2025.

China’s anti-graft watchdog is investigating ​Chen for “suspected severe violations of discipline and laws”, Xinhua said, using a common euphemism for corruption.

For Chinese officials, especially those of Chen’s ⁠rank, the public announcement of an investigation by the central commission for discipline inspection generally signals their eventual political downfall.

The investigation marks a further escalation in President Xi Jinping’s widening anti-graft campaign, which has thinned the party’s senior leadership ranks and depleted the military’s top command.

Before the announcement of the Chen probe, three politburo members from the once 24-member body formed in 2022 – He Weidong, Zhang ⁠Youxia and Ma Xingrui – [had already been purged](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/jan/26/china-top-ranking-general-zhang-youxia-investigation).

Chen, 62, had an unusual rise through China’s official ranks. ​An environmental scientist by training, he earned a doctorate from Imperial ‌College London and rose through China’s elite Tsinghua ‌University to become its president.

He entered government as China’s environmental protection minister in 2015 – just as Xi was elevating pollution control and ecological protection as ‌policy priorities – before becoming mayor of Beijing. He joined the politburo in 2022 and was named party boss of Shanghai, China’s financial hub.

Joseph Torigian, an expert in Chinese politics at American University, called it a reminder of “how little we really understand about what’s going on in Chinese elite politics”.

At a gathering of leaders last month, the ruling Communist party pledged to keep [waging indefinitely its high-pressure anti-corruption campaign](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/26/xi-jinping-corruption-crackdown-china-fifth-plenum), which has ensnared millions within ‌China’s vast bureaucracy and has seen [hundreds of top officials purged](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/30/china-expels-record-number-communist-party-xi-jinping-purges-officials-fifth-plenum), including those once thought untouchable.

Xi had called on the party to “turn the blade inward” and unleash a revolution on itself and eradicate “viruses and impurities” that corrode its health. The party views ​the drive as essential to ensuring its long-term survival.

“No matter who they are, how high their position, or how great their contributions, anyone who engages in corruption will surely receive no leniency,” Xi said in January.

Huawei convicted of stealing trade secrets by US jury Skip to content
Chinese tech giant Huawei was already banned from selling 5G networking tech in the US Image: Mark Schiefelbein/AP Photo/picture alliance Advertisement A US jury convicted Chinese tech giant Huawei on a slew of charges on Tuesday including stealing trade secrets and violating sanctions.
The jury in the Brooklyn federal court found the company guilty on 10 of the 12 criminal counts that it faced, which also included bank fraud and wire fraud.
"For decades, Huawei and three of its subsidiaries conducted their business in the United States on the basis of lies and theft," US Attorney General Todd Blanche said after the verdict.
However, the jury acquitted Huawei on two charges of racketeering and conspiring to obstruct justice.
The verdict is the latest blow to the Chinese tech giant which has for years been banned from selling networking devices to telecom carries in the US and other Western countries . However, its consumer electronics business has continued to grow as its networking business in other countries.
Stolen source code, antenna technology and robot tech
Prosecutors detailed a number of ways Huawei stole trade secrets from competitors in order to undercut them in the market.
In once instance, a Huawei employee slipped into a competitor's booth at a Chicago trade fair in order to photograph circuitboards inside another company's networking divice.
Huawei was also found to have once sold routers containing source code from a rival company.
How the China-US AI arms race is escalating
Prosecutors also said a Huawei employee once removed a robotic arm from a competitor's lab so it could be photographed and measured.
According to court records, the victim companies included Cisco Systems, Motorola Solutions, T-Mobile , Quintel USA and Fujitsu.
"The misappropriated intellectual property included trade secret information and copyrighted works, such as source code and user manuals for internet routers, antenna technology, and robot testing technology," the Department of Justice said.
Prosecutors also alleged that Huawei did business in countries subject to US sanctions including Iran and North Korea .
Huawei then made false statements to both US government officials and banks in order to hide this activity, prosecutors said.
"Few crimes are as serious as Huawei's decades-long pattern of endangering US national security, violating the sanctity of US commerce, and impeding the ‌enforcement of ​US laws," US Attorney Joseph Nocella said.
Huawei continued to deny the allegations even after the verdict on Tuesday.
"We believe the government's remaining charges are equally without legal or factual merit," the company said in a statement.
"The five trade secret-related disputes cited by the government were all civil matters that were resolved over the past two decades. No court ever found Huawei liable for willful intellectual property misappropriation, and the company was never ordered to pay damages for trade secret misappropriation."
The company's lawyer, Brian Heberlig, said: "We fully expect to appeal."
Huawei is set to be sentenced next September and could face billions of dollars in penalties.

Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, was joined on stage in Ottawa by a [Donald Trump](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/donaldtrump) impersonator who mocked the US president to raucous laughter from a crowd of politicians and journalists at a parliamentary press gallery dinner on Saturday.

With coiffed hair and an ill-fitting suit, comedian Mark Critch – who portrays the president on the sketch show This Hour Has 22 Minutes – danced on to the stage and lampooned the trade war Trump started as well as the president’s threats to annex [Canada](https://www.theguardian.com/world/canada).

“We’re going to have a great deal,” Critch said, channeling Trump’s distinct mannerisms. “There’s only one thing standing in the way: me, because I’m crazy.”

The fake Trump continued that he was “so popular we just had a big, blue wave”, a reference to the Democratic rout of Republicans in this month’s US midterm elections.

He also mocked Trump’s frequent mentions of other men’s physiques, saying of the comedian Mark McKinney, who was portraying Carney, that he had “a great ass – doesn’t he? What a beautiful ass, he’s got such an incredible ass.”

He earned the most laughter of his short appearance for saying of Carney: “I don’t call him the governor to his face, because I’m a coward”. The real Trump has frequently attempted to insult Canada’s leaders by calling them governor, not prime minister, suggesting Canada is a US state.

The annual dinner, attended by media, political leaders and lobbyists, is often defined by carefully written jokes by the staff of party leaders.

Throughout his own 16-minute set, Carney poked fun at his political rivals, the media and the US president.

At one point, he remarked: “Damn, this is a tough room, and I’ve been in the Oval Office. Alone. With its new interior decorator.”

Clips of the dinner, including the crowd laughing at the president, have circulated widely on US media.

The newly appointed governor general, Louise Arbour, also gave a speech, including a nod to the prime minister’s decision to travel extensively around the globe.

“Our prime minister is already getting a lot of attention. Actually, I heard a guy the other day compare him to God. Now seriously, do you know the difference between God and [Mark Carney](https://www.theguardian.com/world/mark-carney)? God is everywhere, and Mark Carney is everywhere except in Ottawa where he’s supposed to be,” she said.

The Conservative leader, Pierre Poilievre, also used the evening to poke fun at his own reputation.

“Some say that Mark has a controlling leadership style. There’s been reports that he yells and micromanages his staff. He acts like a miserable prick to journalists,” he said. “And when I hear things like that, I say once again, he’s stealing all my ideas.”

He attracted a stunned silence, however, for alluding to Justin Trudeau’s relationship with Katy Perry, saying, “Trudeau is running around the world doing to a faded pop princess what he did to Canada” while prime minister, a remark that was widely criticised as demeaning to the pop star.

The New Democratic party leader, Avi Lewis, who has not yet won a seat in parliament, took a shot at Carney’s early exit from the event, as well his own party’s dismal standings. “I do not have a seat in the House of Commons, but when I am given one at dinner, I stay there all night long,” he said.

Justice Department Clarifies Lawful Use of Drone Detection Technologies to Protect Americans from Emerging UAS Threats
The Department of Justice today issued an opinion concluding that law enforcement may deploy a broad range of technologies to detect unmanned aircraft systems (“UAS,” commonly called drones) consistent with federal law. The opinion provides critical guidance to federal, state, local, tribal, and territorial authorities working to identify and respond to emerging drone threats while respecting the privacy rights of Americans.
Specifically, the opinion examines the application of the Pen-Trap Statute and the Wiretap Act to drone-detection technologies—including acoustic, electro-optical and infrared (EO/IR), radar, and radiofrequency detection systems—used by state, local, tribal, territorial, and federal law enforcement to protect the public from drone surveillance and other drone threats.
“Drones present extraordinary opportunities for innovation, commerce, and public safety, but they also can be exploited by criminals, foreign adversaries, and other malicious actors,” explained T. Elliot Gaiser, Assistant Attorney General for the Office of Legal Counsel, who signed the opinion. “Today, DOJ provides renewed legal clarity that will help law enforcement detect and defeat drone threats to the safety and privacy of the American people.”
The opinion recognizes that hostile or unlawful drone activity can threaten critical infrastructure, public events, correctional facilities, and other sensitive locations. Such hostile drone activity may also invade the privacy of American citizens. The opinion carefully analyzes federal law to ensure that law enforcement can deploy drone detection technologies in a manner consistent with longstanding statutory protections for radio and electronic communications.
The opinion reaches several key conclusions about the use of drone detection technologies by law enforcement:
Acoustic, electro-optical and infrared, and radar-based drone detection technologies generally do not violate either the Pen-Trap Statute or the Wiretap Act because they do not capture communications metadata or intercept protected communication contents.
Radiofrequency detection systems used to identify drone activity generally do not violate the Pen-Trap Statute so long as they are not attached or applied to a telephone line or other communications facility.
The use of radiofrequency systems for spectrum monitoring and the interception of FAA-required remote identification broadcasts generally does not violate the Wiretap Act because such broadcasts are designed to be publicly accessible.
Whether interception of other drone-related communications complies with the Wiretap Act depends on the particular technology and communications involved and must be assessed on a case-by-case basis.
Strengthening Security While Preserving Privacy
The opinion makes clear that federal, state, local, tribal, and territorial officials can use many widely available detection technologies to identify and track potentially dangerous drone activity without intruding on federally protected communications. It also emphasizes that technologies capable of obtaining the contents of drone communications remain subject to important statutory limitations and, in some circumstances, may require additional legal authority.

Published Time: 2026-11-26T03:41:27+08:00

Markdown Content:
A fire erupted in Egypt’s capital on Wednesday, killing at least 30 people, according to the health ministry, after a fuel truck reportedly overturned on a packed highway.

Footage shot by passers-by showed a massive blaze and huge clouds of smoke rising from the site in Cairo’s densely populated Al-Waraq neighbourhood in Imbaba district.

State media reported that the fire broke out when a truck loaded with fuel overturned on a crowded highway.

The health ministry said 39 ambulances were sent to the scene, and 15 people were taken to hospital with injuries.

Images from the site showed a grisly aftermath, with cars burnt out from the blaze apparently caused by the fuel truck overturning, as firefighters doused the truck’s wreckage.

![Image 1: Flames are seen in the Al-Waraq neighbourhood of Imbaba district in Cairo, Egypt, on Wednesday. Photo: UGC via AFP](https://img.i-scmp.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=contain,width=1024,format=auto/sites/default/files/d8/images/canvas/2026/11/26/39e246c1-b553-4234-a5b7-82b4cc29cf31_21638030.jpg)

Flames are seen in the Al-Waraq neighbourhood of Imbaba district in Cairo, Egypt, on Wednesday. Photo: UGC via AFP

A crowd and emergency services gathered at the scene as a bulldozer removed a car’s burnt-out wreckage, images showed.

Egypt, with its informal residential areas and often dilapidated infrastructure, has suffered several deadly fires in recent years.

Slow response times of emergency services are not unusual in the country, where neighbourhood residents routinely improvise rescue efforts, even within the megalopolis of Cairo.

Fire escapes, smoke detectors and alarms are rare and in many areas, warrens of narrow roads make it hard for fire engines to reach disaster sites.

Car crashes are also common, and often blamed on reckless driving, poor maintenance and uneven law enforcement, with traffic laws also being widely flouted.

Last year, nearly 6,000 people died in road accidents across the country, according to Egypt’s state statistics agency.

The year before, more than 5,200 road deaths were recorded across the country.

In August, at least 18 people, many of them teenagers, were killed in northern Egypt when two pickup trucks carrying agricultural day-labourers crashed.
